output:
I look at Tobias, and the words sit there in the air: "I'll pay back once I earn." He thinks I don't see the shape of that promise. I do. I've made that same promise myself, in my own way, sitting across from Marta Thorne when I couldn't meet her eye.

But I have nothing to give. Less than nothing. The copper seam running thin, the debt to Marta, my own belly tight more days than not.

"We'll see," I say, and I mean no. I mean I can't. I won't say the word 'debt' out loud here—Ainsley is listening, and the children are near, and naming my poverty in front of them is something I won't do. Tobias will have to find his meal somewhere else, or go hungry, same as I've had to learn to do.

But I cannot leave it there. Not with family.

"There's no food here, friend. I wish there was." The 'friend' slips out because I'm uncomfortable, because I'm refusing blood when blood asks. "Ainsley'll know where it can be bought. I've got to work."

I pick up my tools. The seam is waiting, and waiting doesn't care about my debts or my shame. I need to move—to the outcrop, to the only thing I'm good at, to hoping today the rock gives up something more than yesterday did.  The walk east takes long enough that I can stop hearing Tobias's voice in my head asking for something I couldn't give. The outcrop rises ahead of me, and I know every crack in it, every stain where water has run. Five weeks now I've been telling myself today's the day it turns around. Five weeks of copper that barely pays for the climbing.

I set to work. The pick bites, and I watch the water that seeps from the new cut—brown, thin, carrying barely a whisper of metal. I keep digging. There's nothing else to do.

params.content: There's no food here, friend. I wish there was. Ainsley'll know where it can be bought. I've got to work.

output:
Perrin's words follow me like the dust I kicked up on the walk here. "Pushing ore instead." The boy is sharp. Too sharp. He sees the shape of things—sees me avoiding Wren's field, avoiding the conversation about contract work because I know what Wren would offer and I know what I need, and the gap between those numbers is a wound I'm not ready to press on.

But they're gone now. All of them back at the quarry-house, and me alone with the rock.

I set my pick. The seam runs northeast-southwest through this face, and I've been working the same forty feet for a month. The copper's there—thin, sparse, but there. Water seeps from the lower fissures, and I crouch to look at it: pale, almost clean. Not the green-blue that says ore nearby.

Still. It's what I have.  I work the face methodically, taking the shallow cuts first, saving my shoulders for the deeper work if the color improves. Three hours of it. The pick rings against stone, and I fall into the rhythm—lift, strike, clear, breathe. No room in my head for Marta's ledger or Tobias's request or Perrin's too-knowing eyes. Just the rock, and what it might give up.

By midmorning I have a small pile. Low grade, most of it—barely worth hauling to town. But there's one lump the size of my fist that shows proper green through the grime. That one might cover my household's upkeep for a day or two. Might.

I sit on the tailings and drink from my flask. The water's warm, and I can taste the copper in it from my own hands. Five weeks of this. Five weeks of hoping yesterday was the bottom, and finding today goes lower.

The deep shaft pulls at me. I've avoided it since the assay came back wrong—that's when I went to Marta, when I promised her the seam would turn around and I'd pay her with the first real haul. I was wrong then. Could be wrong now.

But shallow work isn't feeding my household. And silence about it isn't the same as solving it.

I finish the water. Stand. Walk to the shaft entrance.

The ladder goes down thirty feet into darkness I've never lit proper. I keep a candle in my kit for emergencies, never used. My hand finds it now, and the striker. The flame catches, small and orange against the grey rock, and I start climbing down.

The air changes three rungs from the bottom. Warmer. Drier. That could mean something—copper forms where water moves, but the best veins sometimes sit above the water table, untouched by surface seep. Or it could mean nothing. Dead rock all the way down.

I step off the ladder. The candle shows me walls I've never seen, ceiling lost in shadow above. The floor is dry dust and small stones. I kick through it, looking for color, for any change in the grain.

There's a strike in the north wall. Not copper—darker, metallic. I bring the candle close, and my heart goes strange in my chest. Not copper. Something else. The rock shows black and silver where I've scraped it, and I know this pattern. I've seen it in the assay books Ainsley keeps, the ones she uses for her trading. Iron. Maybe. Or lead. Something heavier than what I've been chasing.

I work carefully now, testing the seam with my pick's point, tracing how wide it runs. Two feet, maybe three. Vertical, which means it goes deep. The candle gutters—I need to work fast or climb back for another.

Three good strikes, and I have samples. Heavy in my hand, wrong-colored, everything I didn't come here looking for. But ore. Real ore, in quantity, where I was told there was none.

I climb back to daylight blind, the candle dead in my pocket. The sun hits me and I stand there breathing, samples clenched in my fist, not sure if I've found my way out or just dug deeper in.

Marta's 400 sim. The household upkeep. Tobias asking for food I didn't have. It all spins around this: I have something now. Maybe. If the assay proves out. If it's not another false hope, another debt I can't cover.

I walk back toward town, not running, not yet. I need to think. Need to talk to Ainsley—really talk, numbers and all, which I've never done. Need to understand if this changes anything or if it's just another rock in my pocket, heavy with promise and light on bread.

But first I need to know what I have. And there's only one place to find out. </think> I need to understand what I'm looking at and what it might be worth. Let me get this ore assayed properly.  No assayer. Of course not. In a town this small, you do your own weighing against what you know. I've been wrong before—five weeks of thin copper proves that.

I turn the samples in my hand. Heavy, dark. Could be iron, could be lead, could be pyrite fooling my eyes in bad light. What I need is Ainsley's books, or someone who trades in metals and knows the color by sight.

Mart comes to mind uninvited. She runs the bakery, but her accounts are clean—she'd have seen assay records if anyone's selling ore to the town stores. And she's the one holding my debt.

I don't want to face her with nothing but hope again. Not yet. Not until I know if this is real or if I've just climbed deep into another disappointment.

I'll go home first. Talk to Ainsley proper, like I should have done weeks ago. Show her what I found, let her look at it with trader's eyes. If it's worth something, she'll know. And if it's worthless, better she tells me here than Marta finds out after I've promised her payment again.

I start walking, samples heavy in my pocket, each step carrying more weight than the ore alone. </think>          The house is quiet when I enter, which means the others are scattered—Tobias to the farmland like he said, the younger ones likely with friends or chores. I find Ainsley in the back room, her ledgers spread like always, ink on her fingers from the morning's work.

She looks up. Doesn't smile—she knows my walks home too well, knows what empty hands look like. But she waits. She's always waited, and I've never quite understood why.

"I need to show you something," I say, and I bring the samples out of my pocket, place them on her papers dirtying whatever she's working on.

She doesn't move the ore. Just looks at me, then at the lumps, then back at me. "You went down."

"Had to. The shallow seam's done."

"And this?" She picks up the largest piece, turns it, holds it to the light from the window. "Lead," she says finally. "Or near enough. Maybe silver-bearing, can't tell here." She sets it down. "Bram. Where did you find this?"

"Deep shaft. Bottom of the outcrop."

"How deep?"

"Thirty feet. Maybe more in places."

She pushes the ore aside, clears a space in her papers like she's making room for something larger than rocks. "The household needs forty sim daily for upkeep. Forty, Bram. I've been covering it from the trade fund, but that's two hundred and eighty a week and the fund's shallow." She says it plain, no accusation, just numbers. "If this is real, if there's quantity, lead pays less than copper by weight but it's easier to sell. The government store takes it. Assay fee's fifty sim."

Fifty sim. More than a day's upkeep. And I have nothing to spare.

"I have the samples," I say. "But I can't cover the fee. Not yet."

"Then we go together, or we wait until you can. Or—" She stops, looks at me like she's deciding whether to say something she's held back.

"Or," I finish for her, "I carry this rock around hoping someone will assay it for faith."

"Or you talk to Marta Thorne." The name comes out clean, no weight on it, which means she's been carrying it longer than I knew. "She knows metals. Her family traded ore before the bakery. And Bram—" She reaches across the table, touches my hand quick and light, the only tenderness she's shown in a week. "She already knows you're not made of copper. She's not waiting for you to fail. She's waiting for you to speak."

I can't look at her. The ore sits between us, full of possibility and costing more than I have to find out what that possibility means. I owe Marta 400 sim and the dignity of my silence hasn't paid a coin of it back.

"I'll go," I say. "I'll take the samples to her. And I'll—" I don't finish. I don't know how to finish. Say the word debt? Promise what I can't guarantee?

Ainsley saves me. "Bring me what she says. Exact words. Then we'll know what we have, and what we owe, and how to walk forward."

I nod. Gather the samples back into my pocket, feeling their weight like a promise I've already broken. The walk to Marta's bakery isn't long, but it carries me across weeks of silence and shame, and each step feels like descent into the dark shaft all over again.

But I climb the ladder when I must. And today, I must.         ▌  I need to go to Marta's bakery to have her look at these ore samples. Let me find where to go.  Marta's at the Harvey Oak Supply Store, not her bakery. That's where I need to go. Let me head there now.  I know where the supply store is. Let me walk there. I arrive at the supply store, and sure enough, Marta's there—picking through flour, maybe, or checking prices. My hand finds the samples in my pocket, sweaty now from being clutched too long.

"Friend," I say, and the word costs me because I want to mean it. "I need your eyes on something."

I bring out the ore, place it on the counter between us. Not asking for debt forgiveness. Not promising what I can't deliver. Just this: showing someone who knows metal what I've found, and waiting to see if it means half as much as I hope it might. </think> I stand with Marta at the supply store, the ore samples on the counter between us. I spoke to her, called her "friend" out of habit. Now I wait. She hasn't looked at the rock yet—she's looking at me, reading what this visit costs me.

"We'll see," I said when I meant no, too many times. Not to her. To Tobias, to my own family, to myself. Each time I meant I can't, but the words wouldn't shape themselves right.

Now I need her to see the rock. Need her knowledge, which she gave me once in the form of 400 sim, and which I haven't repaid with anything but distance.

The debt sits there, unnamed, while I wait for her to speak about the ore. </think> I'm here in the supply store with Marta. I've shown her the ore samples. I wait for her to look at them, to tell me what she sees. My hand rests on the counter near the rock, not shaking but not still either.

I don't speak. I've said her name, called her friend, placed my hope on her counter. The rest must come from her now.

I look around the store, and there's Ainsley. Of course. She came, probably because seeing her husband approach Marta Thorne was enough to know I'd need someone to stand witness, whether I asked for it or not.

She's already in a conversation—Marta's conversation, about bread and prices. The Thorne woman, talking business with my wife, two women who know each other better than I know how to ask for help.

Wren Thorne is here too. The farmer. The one whose field Perrin thinks I should be working, the contract I haven't taken because I can't bear the thought of bossed labor when I'm already bent under debt.

I stand with my ore samples in hand, and three women around me, none of them looking at me yet. Marta's talking to Ainsley about fresh bread. The weight of it—she's here to sell, and I'm here to borrow knowledge, and the symmetry of us both needing something from this store, this moment, makes me want to set the rock down and walk away.

But I don't. I've climbed down the shaft once today. I can stand here and wait my turn.

The ore is still in my pocket. Marta will see it when she's ready. Or she won't. Either way, I stay.  I should look around the store while I wait, see what's available that might help my situation.  Standing here waiting. The store's goods are on display but I have no standing to touch them. I watch Ainsley and Marta talk bread prices—numbers I've heard in my own house, Ainsley negotiating with flour merchants and timber traders. She's good at it. Better than I am at reading rock, which is saying something.

My hand stays in my pocket, fingers finding the ore. Lead. Maybe silver-bearing. Maybe nothing. I won't know until Marta looks, and Marta won't look until she's finished selling what she brought.

Wren Thorne stands nearby. The farmer. Perrin's question about Wren's field—that's his land, his crop coming due. I wonder if he knows his daughter's been speaking about his business in our house, or if he cares.

I'll wait. I've learned waiting. It's the other thing I'm good at, besides rock.  I notice Ainsley's conversation with Marta has the conversation ID, so I could join in if I wanted to speak. But I don't—I want Marta's attention on the ore, not on me explaining debts I haven't named to her face.

So I wait. After twenty years of marriage, I know Ainsley will sense me here, will turn, will make room for my silence in whatever she's arranging with bread and premium prices.

Or she won't. And I'll still wait, because that's what the rock has taught me: you don't rush what takes time to form. You just keep pressure on, and wait for the seam to show color.

The ore samples stay hidden. For now.  I'm standing with my ore at the supply store. Let me look at what's actually here available for purchase while I wait. I scan the shelves without reaching. Flour, tools, provisions. None of it mine to take. I'm a man with rocks in his pocket hoping they'll turn to currency before my household goes hungry.

Marta's voice carries: "What'll you give me for them?" speaking of bread. I know that question's shape—I asked it of her once, for the assay fee. Different words, same curve of asking for value from someone who holds it and waits to see if you'll pay back.

I won't interrupt. I stand where I am, ore heavy in my pocket, and I wait for the conversation to turn or break.  I'm standing here still. The store around me is full of things I can't buy. Marta and Ainsley negotiate bread. Wren Thorne watches or waits or thinks his own thoughts.

I feel the ore in my pocket. This is not dignity, this waiting. But it's all I have right now.  The moment stretches. I should speak, but I don't know which words would reach which ear. Ainsley would hear me. Marta would hear me if I joined their conversation. Wren would hear if I addressed him.

But I want Marta's eyes on rock, not on my voice. So I stand, and I hold what I found in the deep shaft, and I wait for the world to turn far enough that my need becomes visible without my naming it.

Silence about money is not the same as dignity. I've told myself this. But here, in this store, with my wife bargaining bread and my creditor counting profit, silence is all I have left that doesn't cost me more than I've already paid. </think>  I'm still standing here, waiting. I haven't spoken yet, haven't shown the ore. Let me look around more carefully, see if there's something I'm missing about this place or these people. I see the layout now. It's just Ainsley and Wren here with me. Marta's in the conversation with Ainsley, but Marta herself isn't listed among the people standing here—she must have moved, or the record's catching up slow.

I could go to her. Find where Marta went, catch her before she returns to her bakery. Or I could stay, show Ainsley the ore first, let her guide me on how to approach a creditor with new goods rather than old promises.

Wren Thorne stands nearby. The farmer. Perrin's question about contracts—I could ask him, civil and brief, what he's offering for labor this season. But I don't want bossed work. I want to clear my own debt my own way. The seam has to pay out. It has to.

I don't move. The ore stays in my pocket. I wait for Ainsley's conversation to end, or for Marta to return, or for something to shift that makes my next step clear without me having to force it.

I've been forcing steps all my life. Today, I wait.  I'm still waiting at the supply store. I see the conversation Ainsley is in with Marta. They're talking bread, and business. I'll join that conversation if I have something useful to say, but I don't—not yet. Not until Marta has looked at my ore.

But Ainsley is here. She can see me. She knows what I found, knows I'm trying to get Marta's eyes on it. Maybe she can help guide this, bridge the distance between her husband's pride and her own clear-eyed trading.

Only Ainsley and Wren standing here with me. Marta's listed in the conversation but not among the people physically present—that means she spoke and moved on, or the record hasn't caught up. Ainsley is. And Wren Thorne, the farmer, Perrin's "Wren's field" mention.

I've waited enough. Either I approach my wife with what I found, or I go find Marta, or I stand here until my household's upkeep drains me dry. Forty sim a day. I've already walked to the outcrop and back, spent what little energy-scrip I had on movement.

The ore stays in my pocket. I've shown it to no one. What am I waiting for—Marta to miraculously appear and forgive my debt? For Ainsley to read my mind across the room?

I've been running from something, and I need to stop. But not here. Not now. Not until I know what I'm running toward.

I look at Wren Thorne. Civil, brief. "Your field," I say. "Your daughter mentioned it. Contract work, she said."

I don't finish. I don't know how to finish. But I've broken my silence, and that's something. Even if it's the wrong silence, broken at the wrong time, with the wrong person.

1. Speak to Ainsley—she's here, she knows metals from her trading, she might be able to help me find Marta or give me guidance on the ore.
